Group Analysis of Variable Coefficient
Diffusion–Convection Equations.
II. Contractions and Exact Solutions

N.M. Ivanova †, R.O. Popovych ‡ and C. Sophocleous §

†‡{}^{\dagger}{}^{\ddagger} Institute of Mathematics of NAS of Ukraine, 3 Tereshchenkivska Str., 01601 Kyiv, Ukraine

   e-mail: ivanova@imath.kiev.ua, rop@imath.kiev.ua

‡ Fakultät für Mathematik, Universität Wien, Nordbergstraße 15, A-1090 Wien, Austria

§ Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Cyprus, CY 1678 Nicosia, Cyprus
  e-mail: christod@ucy.ac.cy

This is the second part of the series of papers on symmetry properties of a class of variable coefficient (1+1)-dimensional nonlinear diffusion–convection equations of general form f⁡(x)​ut=(g⁡(x)​A​(u)​ux)x+h⁡(x)​B​(u)​uxf(x)u_{t}=(g(x)A(u)u_{x})_{x}+h(x)B(u)u_{x}. At first, we review the results of [12] on equivalence transformations and group classification of the class under consideration. Investigation of non-trivial limits of parameterized subclasses of equations from the given class, which generate contractions of the corresponding maximal Lie invariance algebras, leads to the natural notion of contractions of systems of differential equations. After a brief discussion on contractions of symmetries, equations and solutions in general case, such types of contractions are studied for diffusion–convection equations. A detailed symmetry analysis of an interesting equation from the class under consideration is performed. Exact solutions of some subclasses of the considered class are also given.

1 Introduction

The present manuscript continues the series of works on symmetry properties of the nonlinear variable-coefficient diffusion–convection equations of form

f⁡(x)​ut=(g⁡(x)​A​(u)​ux)x+h⁡(x)​B​(u)​ux,f(x)u_{t}=(g(x)A(u)u_{x})_{x}+h(x)B(u)u_{x}, (1)

where f=f⁡(x),f=f(x), g=g⁡(x),g=g(x), h=h⁡(x),h=h(x), A=A⁡(u)A=A(u) and B=B⁡(u)B=B(u) are arbitrary smooth functions of their variables, f⁡(x)​g​(x)​A​(u)≠0.f(x)g(x)A(u)\!\neq\!0.

Based on the results on equivalence transformations and group classification adduced in the first part [12] of the presented work, we continue studying Lie group properties of the equations under consideration. Namely, investigation of non-trivial limits of parameterized subclasses of equations from class (1), which generate contractions of the corresponding maximal Lie invariance algebras, leads us to the natural notion of contraction of (systems of) differential equations.

It is well-known that exponential cases of parameter-functions, which admit extensions of maximal Lie invariance algebras, are often limits of the power ones with arbitrary exponents [2, 1, 25]. By analogy with terminology accepted for the Lie algebras we will call such limits as contractions. In such situations some authors exclude exponential cases from formulation of final results of group classification that is correct only under explicit admission of combined usage of both point equivalence transformations and contractions in the framework of group classification. Another famous contraction is one of the 1-dimensional Ricci flow ut=Δ​ln⁡uu_{t}=\Delta\ln u from the porous medium equation ut=m−1​Δ​(um−1)u_{t}=m^{-1}\Delta(u^{m}-1) under the limit m→0m\to 0 [28].

All the above-mentioned contractions were found by ad hoc procedures. To the best of our knowledge this is the first work giving the precise definition and mathematical background for contractions of equations, algebras of symmetries and solutions. The value of the presented theory is illustrated in Section 3 using as example the variable-coefficient diffusion–convection equations (1) investigated.

Such contractions allow us to establish additional connections between different cases of extension of maximal Lie invariance algebra in class (1) and ones between solutions of equations in these cases. Thus, e.g., applying contractions to the known solutions of initial equations one can easily obtain exact solutions of the target equations.

In fact, group analysis (in particular, invariant and partially invariant solutions and solutions obtained from separation of variables) is the only systematic method we know for deducing exact solutions of nonlinear partial differential equations, and the role of exact solutions in our understanding the mechanics and mathematics of mathematical models cannot be over-estimated. Classes of invariant solutions usually include self-similar (automodel) solutions arising from scaling invariance, travelling waves which are invariant with respect to translation symmetries and other classes of solutions having physical and analytical importance. For most of the nonlinear systems invariant solutions are the only available exact solutions.

Below we construct exact solutions of equations from class (1) using different approaches. We start by illustration of the simplest approach for deriving exact solutions of the complicated equations from the ones of a simpler model by means of application of equivalence transformations. At first sight such investigation may seem to be not very interesting and trivial. However, a number of authors investigate symmetry properties of different classes of equivalent equations. In such way they perform a huge number of unnecessary cumbersome calculations. Since equivalence transformations may be quite complicated, sometimes it seems to be impossible to obtain directly complete and correct results for some cases which are equivalent to simple ones, although these results can be easily reconstructed with application of equivalence transformations.

At the same time, it is a general mathematical rule that equivalent in some sense objects possess equivalent properties. In particular, if two systems of equations are equivalent with respect to point transformations then there exists a one-to-one correspondence between their maximal Lie invariance algebras, spaces of conservation laws, potential symmetries, exact solutions etc. All the above mentioned features for more complicated models can be constructed from ones of the simpler equivalent models by means of application of known equivalence transformation easier than by direct calculations.

We performed the classical Lie reduction procedure for an equation that cannot be reduced to a constant coefficient equation from class (1). Then we investigate in more detail an equation having, from the one side, remarkable Lie symmetry property (namely, s​l​(2,ℝ)sl(2,\mathbb{R})-invariance) and, from the other side, admitting application of powerful non-Lie methods of construction of exact solutions.

The present paper is organized as follows. First of all, in Section 2, for convenience of the reader we review (in the most suitable for our purpose form) the results of [12] on equivalence transformations and group classification of equations (1) using simultaneously two different gauges g=1g=1 and g=hg=h. Then, in Section 3 we introduce the notion of contractions of equations and contractions of symmetry algebras, give a necessary theoretical background and found contractions of previously classified diffusion–convection equations and those of corresponding symmetry algebras. Examples of application of additional equivalence transformations are shown in Section 4, where we reconstruct exact solutions of variable coefficient equations with four-dimensional symmetry algebras (reducible to constant coefficient ones) from the known solutions of constant coefficient equations. A case of equation reducible to a constant coefficient form that do not belong to the class under consideration is presented in Section 5. In Section 6 an enhanced group analysis of essentially variable coefficient s​l​(2,ℝ)sl(2,\mathbb{R})-invariant diffusion–convection equation is presented and a set of exact Lie and non-Lie solution is constructed via reduction with respect to the classical Lie and nonclassical symmetries.

Results of Section 3 will be generalized in the third part [13] of this series of papers where we introduce the notion of contractions of conservation laws, study the space of local conservation laws and investigate contractions of the conservation laws of equations from class (1). Ibid we introduce also some generalizations of equivalences of conservation laws that allow us to generalize procedure of construction of potential systems for systems of differential equations. Using this new technique we construct all possible inequivalent potential systems for equations from class (1).

2 Equivalence transformations and group classification
of diffusion–convection equations

In this section we briefly summarize the results of the first part [12] of this series of papers concerning equivalence transformations and group classification of class (1), presenting these results in the most suitable form for our purpose. Due to lack of power of the usual equivalence group G∼G^{\sim} it seems to be impossible to obtain result of group classification of class (1) up to G∼G^{\sim} in explicit form [15]. So, we adduce the extended equivalence group [12, 11] containing transformations depending nonlocally on arbitrary elements. Using the direct method we construct the complete in this sense group G^∼\hat{G}^{\sim} formed by the transformations

t~=δ1​t+δ2,x~=X⁡(x),u~=δ3​u+δ4,\displaystyle\tilde{t}=\delta_{1}t+\delta_{2},\quad\tilde{x}=X(x),\quad\tilde{u}=\delta_{3}u+\delta_{4},
f~=ε1​δ1​φXx​f,g~=ε1​ε2−1​Xx​φ​g,h~=ε1​ε3−1​φ​h,A~=ε2​A,B~=ε3​(B+ε4​A),\displaystyle\tilde{f}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_{1}\delta_{1}\varphi}{X_{x}}f,\quad\tilde{g}=\varepsilon_{1}\varepsilon_{2}^{-1}X_{x}\varphi\,g,\quad\tilde{h}=\varepsilon_{1}\varepsilon_{3}^{-1}\varphi\,h,\quad\tilde{A}=\varepsilon_{2}A,\quad\tilde{B}=\varepsilon_{3}(B+\varepsilon_{4}A),

where δj\delta_{j} (j=1,4¯)(j=\overline{1,4}) and εi\varepsilon_{i} (i=1,4¯)(i=\overline{1,4}) are arbitrary constants, δ1​δ3​ε1​ε2​ε3≠0\delta_{1}\delta_{3}\varepsilon_{1}\varepsilon_{2}\varepsilon_{3}\not=0, XX is an arbitrary smooth function of xx, Xx≠0X_{x}\not=0, φ=e−ε4∫h⁡(x)g⁡(x)dx\varphi=e^{-\varepsilon_{4}\int\frac{h(x)}{g(x)}dx}.

Group G^∼\hat{G}^{\sim} contains a normal subgroup G^∼g\hat{G}^{\sim g} of gauge equivalence transformations [12, 11, 18]

f~=ε1​φ​f,g~=ε1​ε2−1​φ​g,h~=ε1​ε3−1​φ​h,A~=ε2​A,B~=ε3​(B+ε4​A),\displaystyle\tilde{f}=\varepsilon_{1}\varphi\,f,\quad\tilde{g}=\varepsilon_{1}\varepsilon_{2}^{-1}\varphi\,g,\quad\tilde{h}=\varepsilon_{1}\varepsilon_{3}^{-1}\varphi\,h,\quad\tilde{A}=\varepsilon_{2}A,\quad\tilde{B}=\varepsilon_{3}(B+\varepsilon_{4}A), (2)

where φ=e−ε4∫h⁡(x)g⁡(x)dx\varphi=e^{-\varepsilon_{4}\int\frac{h(x)}{g(x)}dx}, εi\varepsilon_{i} (i=1,4¯)(i=\overline{1,4}) are arbitrary constants, ε1​ε2​ε3≠0\varepsilon_{1}\varepsilon_{2}\varepsilon_{3}\not=0 (the variables tt, xx and uu do not transform!). The transformations (2) act only on arbitrary elements and do not really change equations. Application of gauge equivalence transformations is equivalent to rewriting equations in another form. In spite of really equivalence transformations, their role in group classification comes not to choice of representatives in equivalence classes but to choice of form of these representatives.

Choice of a gauge for the arbitrary elements is very important for solving and for the final presentation of results. It is more convenient to constrain the parameter-function gg instead of ff in class (1). The next problem is choice between gauges of gg. Group classification of (1) is performed in [12] in two different gauges: g=1g=1 and g=hg=h. For further investigation we should reduce these results to the floating gauge in order to obtain the simplest representatives in each equivalence class. So, below, in contrast to [12] we adduce the group classification with floating gauge. The cases B∉⟨1,A⟩B\not\in\langle 1,A\rangle and A=1A=1 are investigated in the gauge g=hg=h. In the other cases, to obtain results in a simpler explicit form one should use the gauge g=1g=1.

Theorem 1.

The Lie algebra of the kernel of principal groups of (1) is A∩=⟨∂t⟩A^{\cap}=\langle\partial_{t}\rangle. A complete set of G^∼\hat{G}^{\mathop{\sim}}-inequivalent equations (1) which have the wider Lie invariance algebras than A∩A^{\cap} is exhausted by cases given in tables 1–3.

In tables 1–3 we list all possible G^∼\hat{G}^{\mathop{\sim}}-inequivalent sets of functions f⁡(x),f(x), h⁡(x)h(x) A⁡(u),A(u), B⁡(u)B(u) and corresponding invariance algebras under the gauge g=1g=1 or g=hg=h. Numbers with the same Arabic numerals and different Roman letters correspond to cases that are equivalent with respect to additional equivalence transformations. Explicit formulas for these transformations can be found in [12]. The cases which are contained in tables with different Arabic numbers or are numbered with different Arabic numerals are reciprocally inequivalent with respect to point transformations, except the cases with asterisked numeration, presented here to preserve the same numeration as in [12].

The operators from tables 1–3 form bases of the maximal invariance algebras iff the corresponding sets of the functions ff, hh, AA and BB are G^∼\hat{G}^{\mathop{\sim}}-inequivalent to ones with more extensive invariance algebras. For example, in case 3.1 the adduced operators have the above property iff f≠f3f\not=f^{3}.

3 Contractions of equations and of Lie invariance algebras

In this section we investigate non-trivial limits of parameterized subclasses of equations from class (1), which generate contractions of the corresponding maximal Lie invariance algebras as realizations of abstract Lie algebras in the complete space of (independent and dependent) variables. By analogy with terminology accepted for abstract Lie algebras, we will call such limits of parameterized classes and their Lie symmetries as contractions of equations and Lie invariance algebras correspondingly.

First we introduce some related notions and formulate two simple but very useful statements concerning contractions of equations in the general case.

Consider the class {ℒλ}\{\mathcal{L}^{\lambda}\} of systems ℒλ\mathcal{L}^{\lambda}: L⁡(x,u(p),λ)=0L(x,u_{(p)},\lambda)=0 of ll differential equations for mm unknown functions u=(u1,…,um)u=(u^{1},\ldots,u^{m}) of nn independent variables x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}), which are parameterized with the parameter λ.\lambda. Here u(p)u_{(p)} denotes the set of all derivatives of uu with respect to xx of order not greater than pp, including uu as the derivatives of the zero order. L=(L1,…,Ll)L=(L^{1},\ldots,L^{l}) is a tuple of ll fixed functions depending on x,x, u(p)u_{(p)} and λ\lambda. For simplicity we assume λ\lambda as a single numeric (real or complex) parameter. (Extension to more general case with respect to λ\lambda is obvious.) We also suppose that the systems ℒλ\mathcal{L}^{\lambda} are totally nondegenerate.

Let ℒ^λ={L^k​(x,u(p),λ)=0,k=1,…,l^}\hat{\mathcal{L}}^{\lambda}=\{\hat{L}^{k}(x,u_{(p)},\lambda)=0,\ k=1,\ldots,\hat{l}\} be a maximal set of algebraically independent differential consequences of ℒλ\mathcal{L}^{\lambda} that have, as differential equations, orders not greater than pp. All such sets of differential consequences determine the same manifold ℒ¯λ\bar{\mathcal{L}}^{\lambda} in the jet space J(p)J^{(p)}. Let us fix a value of the parameter λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0} and a point 𝐣0∈ℒ¯λ0{\bf j}_{0}\in\bar{\mathcal{L}}^{\lambda_{0}}.

The systems ℒλ\mathcal{L}^{\lambda} weakly converge to the system ℒλ0\mathcal{L}^{\lambda_{0}} near the point 𝐣0∈ℒ¯λ0{\bf j}_{0}\in\bar{\mathcal{L}}^{\lambda_{0}} under λ→λ0\lambda\to\lambda_{0}, iff for any λ\lambda from a deleted neighborhood Λ\Lambda of λ0\lambda_{0} there exist ℒ^λ\hat{\mathcal{L}}^{\lambda} and an open neighborhood Ω\Omega of 𝐣0{\bf j}_{0} in J(p)J^{(p)} such that

2) if L^k\hat{L}^{k}, k=1,…,l^k=1,\ldots,\hat{l} are extended to λ0\lambda_{0} by continuity then for an l^\hat{l}-element subset of the variables u(p)u_{(p)} the Jacobian |∂L^k/∂vk′|≠0|\partial\hat{L}^{k}/\partial v^{k^{\prime}}|\not=0 on Ω\Omega for any λ\lambda from a neighborhood of λ0\lambda_{0}.

We will use the denotation ℒλ⇀ℒλ0\mathcal{L}^{\lambda}\rightharpoonup\mathcal{L}^{\lambda_{0}}, λ→λ0\lambda\to\lambda_{0}.

Consider the parameterized set {Qλ,λ∈Λ}\{Q^{\lambda},\;\lambda\in\Lambda\} of the operators

on the space of variables (x,u)(x,u) and a fixed operator

Lemma 1.

Let for any λ\lambda from a deleted neighborhood of λ0\lambda_{0} the system ℒλ\mathcal{L}^{\lambda} be Lie invariant with respect to an operator QλQ^{\lambda}, ℒλ⇀ℒλ0\mathcal{L}^{\lambda}\rightharpoonup\mathcal{L}^{\lambda_{0}} and pr(p)Qλ→pr(p)Q0\mathop{\rm pr}\nolimits_{(p)}Q^{\lambda}\to\mathop{\rm pr}\nolimits_{(p)}Q^{0}, λ→λ0\lambda\to\lambda_{0}. Q~λ=Qλ−(λ−λ0)−k​(∑i=0k−1di​Qλd​λi|λ=λ0​(λ−λ0)i),Q~0=dk​Qλd​λk|λ=λ0\tilde{Q}^{\lambda}=Q^{\lambda}-(\lambda-\lambda_{0})^{-k}\biggl(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\dfrac{d^{i}Q^{\lambda}}{d\lambda^{i}}\Bigr|_{\lambda=\lambda_{0}}(\lambda-\lambda_{0})^{i}\biggr),\qquad\tilde{Q}^{0}=\dfrac{d^{k}Q^{\lambda}}{d\lambda^{k}}\Bigr|_{\lambda=\lambda_{0}}

Note 1.

For contracted systems of differential equations we can introduce the notion of contractions of solutions and then investigate connections between contractions of Lie invariant solutions and contractions of corresponding subalgebras of the Lie invariance algebras (see Section 8). It is also possible to consider contractions of involutive sets of reduction operators and solutions which are invariant in the non-classical (conditional) sense. The study of the above contractions and contractions of symmetries and invariant solutions of other kinds will be the subject of our further investigations.

There exists a number of different non-trivial contractions of equations from class (1) and, in particular, equations having wider Lie invariance algebras than the kernel algebra A∩=⟨∂t⟩A^{\cap}=\langle\partial_{t}\rangle. Contractions allow us to find additional connections between different cases of extension of maximal Lie invariance algebra in class (1) and between solutions of equations in these cases.

The simplest contractions are the ones in parameterized subclasses of equations with respect to their parameters. For instance, case 2.2c is the limit of case 2.2b under p→−2p\to-2. The Lie invariance algebra of case 2.2c can be obtained from that of case 2.2b by means of the contraction with p→−2p\to-2:

Q1​p→Q1,Q2​p→Q2,−Q3​p+ε​Q2​p−Q1​pε⁡(p+2)→Q3,p→−2.Q^{1p}\to Q^{1},\quad Q^{2p}\to Q^{2},\quad-\dfrac{Q^{3p}+\varepsilon Q^{2p}-Q^{1p}}{\varepsilon(p+2)}\to Q^{3},\quad p\to-2.

Hereafter the operators are taken from the corresponding tables. The “left-hand-side” (“right-hand-side”) operators are from the given basis of the case which is the object (target) of the contraction. The basic operators are numerated in accordance with their order at the tables.

The above contraction illustrates corollary 1 since Q3​p+ε​Q2​p→Q1​p=Q1Q^{3p}+\varepsilon Q^{2p}\to Q^{1p}=Q^{1}, p→−2p\to-2 and Q1=d⁡(Q3​p+ε​Q2​p)/d​p|p=−2Q^{1}=d(Q^{3p}+\varepsilon Q^{2p})/dp\big|_{p=-2}. The tuples (Q1​p,Q2​p,Q3​p)(Q^{1p},Q^{2p},Q^{3p}) and (Q1,Q2,Q3)(Q^{1},Q^{2},Q^{3}) determine equivalent third-rank realizations of the algebra A2.1⊕A1A_{2.1}\oplus A_{1}. We use the Mubarakzyanov’s notations [19] of low-dimensional solvable real Lie algebras. A1A_{1} denotes the one-dimensional Lie algebra and A2.1A_{2.1} does the non-Abelian two-dimensional Lie algebra. It follows from results of [23] that up to weak equivalence of realizations there exists the unique third-rank realization of the algebra A2.1⊕A1A_{2.1}\oplus A_{1}. Therefore, equivalence of realizations ⟨Q1​p,Q2​p,Q3​p⟩\langle Q^{1p},Q^{2p},Q^{3p}\rangle and ⟨Q1,Q2,Q3⟩\langle Q^{1},Q^{2},Q^{3}\rangle is foreknown.

4 Construction of exact solutions
via equivalence transformations

Results of group classification and additional equivalence transformations can be used for construction of exact solutions of equations from class (1) admitting extensions of maximal Lie invariance group. In [24, 15] known exact solutions of “constant coefficient” diffusion–convection equations were mapped to ones of variable coefficient equations (1) by means of additional equivalence transformations.

In view of Theorem 5 of [12] if an equation of form (1) is invariant with respect to a Lie algebra of dimension not less than 4 then it can be reduced by point transformations to one with f=g=h=1f=g=h=1. Therefore, we can reconstruct solutions of these variable-coefficient equations from the already known solutions using additional equivalence transformations found in [12]. Thus, e.g., equation 3.2g

ex​ut=(u−1​ux)x+ε​ex​uxe^{x}u_{t}=(u^{-1}u_{x})_{x}+\varepsilon e^{x}u_{x} (3)

can be transformed to the fast diffusion equation ut=(u−1​ux)xu_{t}=(u^{-1}u_{x})_{x} with the point transformation

t~=eε​t/ε,x~=x+ε​t,u~=ex+ε​t​u.\tilde{t}=e^{\varepsilon t}/\varepsilon,\quad\tilde{x}=x+\varepsilon t,\quad\tilde{u}=e^{x+\varepsilon t}u. (4)

The list of known GmaxG^{\max}-inequivalent Lie solutions of the fast diffusion equation is exhausted by the following ones [26]:

The lists of known exact solutions and Lie reductions of the constant coefficient and some of the variable coefficient equations can be found, e.g., in [10, 21]. Using them one can easily obtain exact solutions of any of the variable coefficient equations having the Lie symmetry algebra of dimension not less then 4. Since the solutions of these equations can be reconstructed from ones presented in other sections, we can turn back to the more interesting cases.

5 Example of Lie reduction

In this section we consider in more details Lie reductions of variable coefficient equation 3.2

ep​x2​ut=(ep​x2​ux)x+ep​x2​u​ux,e^{px^{2}}u_{t}=(e^{px^{2}}u_{x})_{x}+e^{px^{2}}uu_{x}, (6)

which is invariant with respect to the three-dimensional Lie symmetry algebra

⟨∂t,e−2​p​t∂x,∂x−2p∂u⟩.\langle\partial_{t},\,e^{-2pt}\partial_{x},\,\partial_{x}-2p\partial_{u}\rangle.

In contrast to the case of equations with four-dimensional Lie symmetry algebra we cannot reduce equation (6) to an equation of form (1) with f=g=h=1f=g=h=1. However, it is an interesting feature of this equation that using a point transformation v=u+2​p​xv=u+2px it can be mapped to a constant coefficient reaction–convection–diffusion equation

vt=vx​x+v​vx−2​p​vv_{t}=v_{xx}+vv_{x}-2pv (7)

that does not belong to class (1). Similarly to Section 4 for simplification of the technical calculations we will investigate the constant coefficient equation (7) instead of (6). The Lie symmetry algebra of equation (7)

⟨X1=∂t,X2=e−2​p​t(∂x+2p∂v),X3=∂x⟩\langle X_{1}=\partial_{t},\,X_{2}=e^{-2pt}(\partial_{x}+2p\partial_{v}),\,X_{3}=\partial_{x}\rangle

is a realization of A2.1⊕A1A_{2.1}\oplus A_{1} [19]. These operators generate the following group of point transformations:

t~=t+ε1,x~=x+ε2​e−2​p​t+ε3,v~=v+2​ε2​p​e−2​p​t.\tilde{t}=t+\varepsilon_{1},\quad\tilde{x}=x+\varepsilon_{2}e^{-2pt}+\varepsilon_{3},\quad\tilde{v}=v+2\varepsilon_{2}pe^{-2pt}.

A list of proper inequivalent subalgebras of the given algebra is exhausted by the following ones

⟨X1+α​X3⟩,⟨X3+ε​X2⟩,⟨X2⟩,⟨X1,X3⟩,⟨X2,X3⟩,⟨X1+β​X3,X2⟩,\langle X_{1}+\alpha X_{3}\rangle,\quad\langle X_{3}+\varepsilon X_{2}\rangle,\quad\langle X_{2}\rangle,\quad\langle X_{1},\,X_{3}\rangle,\quad\langle X_{2},\,X_{3}\rangle,\quad\langle X_{1}+\beta X_{3},\,X_{2}\rangle,

where α\alpha and β\beta are arbitrary constants, ε=0,±1\varepsilon=0,\pm 1 [20].

The first three (one-dimensional) subalgebras lead to Lie reductions to ordinary differential equations, the fourth and sixth (two-dimensional) ones yield reductions to algebraic equations. Lie reductions with respect to these subalgebras are summarized in table 4. One can easily check that it is impossible to construct a Lie ansatz corresponding to the subalgebra ⟨X2,X3⟩\langle X_{2},\,X_{3}\rangle.

Ansatzes 4.2 and 4.3 give a hint for a possible form

v=φ⁡(t)​x+ψ⁡(t)v=\varphi(t)x+\psi(t)

Note 2.

Using the point transformation t~=e−2​p​t\tilde{t}=e^{-2pt}, x~=x\tilde{x}=x, v~=e2​p​t​v\tilde{v}=e^{2pt}v equation (7) can be mapped to a variable coefficient Burgers equation v~t~=−2​p​t~−1​v~x~​x~−2​p​v~​v~x~\tilde{v}_{\tilde{t}}=-2p{\tilde{t}}^{-1}\tilde{v}_{\tilde{x}\tilde{x}}-2p\tilde{v}\tilde{v}_{\tilde{x}} studied in [17].

Note 3.

The well-known Cole–Hopf transformation v=2​wx/wv=2w_{x}/w reduces equation (7) to the famous constant coefficient reaction–diffusion equation with weak nonlinearity

wt=wx​x−2​p​w​ln⁡|w|.w_{t}=w_{xx}-2pw\ln|w|.

After application of the Cole–Hopf transformation to the list of known exact solutions (see, e.g., [21]) of the equation with weak nonlinearity we obtain exactly solutions (8) of equation (7).

In this and previous sections we have constructed exact solutions of variable coefficient equations of form (1) reducible to constant coefficient ones which either belong or not to class (1). In the next section we consider an essentially variable coefficient equation that is distinguished with its symmetry properties from class (1).

6 Group analysis of a remarkable 𝒔​𝒍​(𝟐,ℝ)sl(2,\mathbb{R})-invariant
diffusion–convection equation

Analyzing the results of group classification, we can observe a number of G^∼\hat{G}^{\mathop{\sim}}-inequivalent equations (1) which are invariant with respect to different realizations of the algebra s​l​(2,ℝ)sl(2,\mathbb{R}). The set of such equations is practically exhausted by the well-known (“constant coefficient”) Burgers and u−4/3u^{-4/3}-diffusion equations and by the equations which are equivalent to them with respect to additional transformations (cases 3.2 and 3.2). This set is supplemented by the unique essentially variable coefficient equation

x2ut=(u−6/5ux)x+x2uxx^{2}u_{t}=(u^{-6/5}u_{x})_{x}+x^{2}u_{x} (9)

(case 3.2). The s​l​(2,ℝ)sl(2,\mathbb{R})-invariance of (9) is directly connected with the fact that hh is not constant. The corresponding realization of the algebra s​l​(2,ℝ)sl(2,\mathbb{R}) is quite different from ones of cases 3.2 and 3.2 and is the maximal Lie invariance algebra of equation (9). It was the reason for us to study equation (9) from the symmetry point of view in details. Indeed, instead of equation (9) we investigate the simpler equation

x2​vt=v​vx​x−56​(vx)2+x2​vxx^{2}v_{t}=vv_{xx}-\frac{5}{6}(v_{x})^{2}+x^{2}v_{x} (10)

Pt=∂t,D=t∂t+x∂x+3v∂v,Π=t2∂t+(2tx+x2)∂x+6(t+x)v∂v.P_{t}=\partial_{t},\quad D=t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x}+3v\partial_{v},\quad\Pi=t^{2}\partial_{t}+(2tx+x^{2})\partial_{x}+6(t+x)v\partial_{v}.

7 On nonclassical symmetries

Reduction operators (nonclassical symmetries, QQ-conditional symmetries) of equations (1) have the general form Q=τ∂t+ξ∂x+η∂uQ=\tau\partial_{t}+\xi\partial_{x}+\eta\partial_{u}, where τ\tau, ξ\xi and η\eta are functions of tt, xx and uu, and (τ,ξ)≠(0,0)(\tau,\xi)\neq(0,0).

Definition 2.

The differential equation ℒ\mathcal{L} is called conditionally invariant with respect to the operator QQ if the relation Q(r)​L​(t,x,u(r))|ℒ∩𝒬(r)=0Q_{(r)}L(t,x,u_{(r)})\bigl|_{\mathcal{L}\cap\mathcal{Q}^{(r)}}=0 holds, which is called the conditional invariance criterion. Then QQ is called an operator of conditional symmetry (or QQ-conditional symmetry, nonclassical symmetry etc) of the equation ℒ\mathcal{L}.

See, e.g., [31, 26] for necessary definitions and properties of nonclassical symmetries. Since (1) is an evolution equation, there are two principally different cases of finding QQ: τ≠0\tau\neq 0 and τ=0\tau=0.

The problem of classification of nonclassical symmetries with τ≠0\tau\neq 0 is not completely solved even in the case of constant coefficient diffusion–convection equations. However, some particular results are known. Thus, e.g., constant coefficient diffusion equation with power nonlinearity

ut=(uμ​ux)xu_{t}=(u^{\mu}u_{x})_{x}

admits non-classical symmetries only for μ=−1/2\mu=-1/2 [9]. Ibid a particular case of such operators Q=∂t+12x−2u1/2Q=\partial_{t}+12x^{-2}u^{1/2} is adduced and the corresponding exact solution u=(6​t​x−1+C1​x3+C2​x−2)2u=(6tx^{-1}+C_{1}x^{3}+C_{2}x^{-2})^{2} is constructed. Here C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are arbitrary constants. The same solution were found previously in [16]. Conditional symmetry operator Q=∂t−λuμ+1∂xQ=\partial_{t}-\lambda u^{\mu+1}\partial_{x} for the equation ut=(uμ​ux)x+λ​uμ+1​uxu_{t}=(u^{\mu}u_{x})_{x}+\lambda u^{\mu+1}u_{x} is found in the recent work [3]. Constant coefficient diffusion equation with exponential nonlinearity ut=(eu​ux)xu_{t}=(e^{u}u_{x})_{x} admits two inequivalent reduction operators: Q=x∂t+eu∂uQ=x\partial_{t}+e^{u}\partial_{u} and Q=x2∂t+2xeu∂x+2eu∂uQ=x^{2}\partial_{t}+2xe^{u}\partial_{x}+2e^{u}\partial_{u} [6, 7].

We derive the system of determining equations for the reduction operators with τ≠0\tau\neq 0 of equations (1):

Example 1.

A=B=u−1/2A=B=u^{-1/2}, ∀f⁡(x),h⁡(x)\forall f(x),h(x), g⁡(x)=1g(x)=1: Q=∂t+ϕu∂xQ=\partial_{t}+\phi\sqrt{u}\partial_{x}, where ϕ=ϕ⁡(x)\phi=\phi(x) is an arbitrary solution of equation

ϕ′′+h⁡(x)​ϕ′−1/2​f​(x)​ϕ2=0.\phi^{\prime\prime}+h(x)\phi^{\prime}-1/2f(x)\phi^{2}=0.

Similarly we found an example of nonclassical symmetry in the case of exponential nonlinearities.

Example 2.

A=B=euA=B=e^{u}, ∂t+ϕ(x)eu∂x\partial_{t}+\phi(x)e^{u}\partial_{x}, where ϕ′−f​ϕ2−h​ϕ=0\phi^{\prime}-f\phi^{2}-h\phi=0.

As well-known, the operators with the vanishing coefficient of ∂t\partial_{t} form so-called “no-go” case in study of conditional symmetries of an arbitrary (1 + 1)-dimensional evolution equation since the problem on their finding is reduced to a single equation which is equivalent to the initial one (see e.g[8, 22, 30]). Note that “no-go” case has to be treated as impossibility only of exhaustive solving of the problem. A number of particular examples of reduction operators with τ=0\tau=0 can be constructed under additional constraints and then applied to finding exact solutions of the initial equation. Since the determining equation has more independent variables and, therefore, more degrees of freedom, it is more convenient often to guess a simple solution or a simple ansatz for the determining equation, which can give a parametric set of complicated solutions of the initial equation. Namely, in the case τ=0\tau=0 we have ξ≠0\xi\neq 0. Up to usual equivalence of reduction operators, ξ\xi can be assumed equal to 1, i.e. Q=∂x+η∂uQ=\partial_{x}+\eta\partial_{u}. The conditional invariance criterion implies the determining equation on the coefficient η\eta

ηt​f2−2​η​ηu​x​f​A−η2​ηu​u​f​A−2​η2​ηu​f​Au+η​ηu​fx​A−ηx​x​f​A−3​η​ηx​f​Au+ηx​fx​A\displaystyle\eta_{t}f^{2}-2\eta\eta_{ux}fA-\eta^{2}\eta_{uu}fA-2\eta^{2}\eta_{u}fA_{u}+\eta\eta_{u}f_{x}A-\eta_{xx}fA-3\eta\eta_{x}fA_{u}+\eta_{x}f_{x}A
−ηx​f​h​B−η3​f​Au​u+η2​fx​Au+η​fx​h​B−η​hx​f​B−η2​f​h​Bu=0\displaystyle-\eta_{x}fhB-\eta^{3}fA_{uu}+\eta^{2}f_{x}A_{u}+\eta f_{x}hB-\eta h_{x}fB-\eta^{2}fhB_{u}=0

which is reduced with a non-point transformation to equation (1), where η\eta becomes a parameter. We have found some partial solutions of the determining equations.

Example 3.

A=BA=B, ∀f\forall f, ∀h\forall h, η=ϕ⁡(x)​A−1\eta=\phi(x)A^{-1}, where ϕ′+h​ϕ=0\phi^{\prime}+h\phi=0.

Example 4.

A=unA=u^{n}, B=u2​nB=u^{2n}, f=x−2f=x^{-2}, h=x−2​(n+1)n+2h=x^{-\frac{2(n+1)}{n+2}}, η=1(n+2)2​x−2n+2​u1−n\eta=\frac{1}{(n+2)^{2}}x^{-\frac{2}{n+2}}u^{1-n}.

8 Contractions of solutions

Consider, as in Section 3, the class {ℒλ}\{\mathcal{L}^{\lambda}\} of totally nondegenerate systems ℒλ\mathcal{L}^{\lambda}: L⁡(x,u(p),λ)=0L(x,u_{(p)},\lambda)=0 of ll differential equations for mm unknown functions u=(u1,…,um)u=(u^{1},\ldots,u^{m}) of nn independent variables x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}), which are parameterized with the (single numeric) parameter λ\lambda.

Let for any λ\lambda from a deleted neighborhood of λ0\lambda_{0} the system ℒλ\mathcal{L}^{\lambda} be Lie invariant with respect to a symmetry algebra AλA^{\lambda}, ℒλ⇀ℒλ0\mathcal{L}^{\lambda}\rightharpoonup\mathcal{L}^{\lambda_{0}} and Aλ→Aλ0A^{\lambda}\to A^{\lambda_{0}}, λ→λ0\lambda\to\lambda_{0}. Then, according to the results of Section 3, the system ℒλ0\mathcal{L}^{\lambda_{0}} is Lie invariant with respect to the algebra Aλ0A^{\lambda_{0}}.

If ωλ\omega^{\lambda} is a Lie ansatz corresponding to the algebra AλA^{\lambda}, then, using the theorems on convergence of solutions of differential equations with respect to initial data and parameters (see, e.g., [4]) one can prove that there exists such ωλ0\omega^{\lambda_{0}} that ωλ→ωλ0\omega^{\lambda}\to\omega^{\lambda_{0}}, λ→λ0\lambda\to\lambda_{0} and ωλ0\omega^{\lambda_{0}} is an Ansatz corresponding to the algebra Aλ0A^{\lambda_{0}}. Consequently the systems reduced with respect to ωλ\omega^{\lambda} converge to one reduced with ωλ0\omega^{\lambda_{0}}. In such sense we can talk about contractions of ansatzes and reduced systems.

Consider an example of contractions of ansatzes, reduced equations and solutions of equations (1). As it is shown above, under the action of contraction u=1+u~μu=1+\frac{\tilde{u}}{\mu}, μ→+∞\mu\to+\infty diffusion equation with power nonlinearity

ut=(uμ​ux)xu_{t}=(u^{\mu}u_{x})_{x} (22)

(case 3.2) invariant with respect to Aμ=⟨Q1μ=∂t,Q2μ=t∂t−μ−1u∂u,Q3μ=∂x,Q4μ=x∂x+2μ−1u∂u⟩A^{\mu}=\langle Q^{\mu}_{1}=\partial_{t},Q^{\mu}_{2}=t\partial_{t}-\mu^{-1}u\partial_{u},Q^{\mu}_{3}=\partial_{x},Q^{\mu}_{4}=x\partial_{x}+2\mu^{-1}u\partial_{u}\rangle is reduced to the equation

u~t=(eu~​u~x)x\tilde{u}_{t}=(e^{\tilde{u}}\tilde{u}_{x})_{x} (23)

(case 2.2) with exponential nonlinearity being invariant with respect to the Lie symmetry algebra Aexp=⟨Q1=∂t,Q2=t∂t−∂u,Q3=∂x,Q4=x∂x+2∂u⟩A^{\exp}=\langle Q_{1}=\partial_{t},Q_{2}=t\partial_{t}-\partial_{u},Q_{3}=\partial_{x},Q_{4}=x\partial_{x}+2\partial_{u}\rangle.

The basis elements of the Lie invariance algebra AexpA^{\exp} can be obtained under the same contraction as Qiμ→QiQ^{\mu}_{i}\to Q_{i}.

9 Conclusion

In this second part of the presented series of papers (see also [12, 13, 14]) we investigate in more detail symmetry properties of class (1). Namely, considering non-trivial limits of parameterized subclasses of equations from class (1), which generate contractions of the corresponding maximal Lie invariance algebras, we introduce the notion of contraction of (systems of) differential equations and consider contractions of equations and from class (1) and ones of their symmetries. We also investigate s​l​(2,ℝ)sl(2,\mathbb{R})-invariant equation (9) which is “essentially variable coefficient” in the sense that it is not reducible to equations of form (1) with constant values of ff, gg and hh.

Using similar techniques, we can study other classes of non-linear evolution equations which are closed to the class under consideration, e.g. the class of variable coefficient reaction–diffusion equations of the general form f⁡(x)​ut=(g⁡(x)​A​(u)​ux)x+h⁡(x)​B​(u)f(x)u_{t}=(g(x)A(u)u_{x})_{x}+h(x)B(u), where all denotations coincide with ones in (1). (See the resent work [27] for its particular case with power nonlinearity.) However, experience of modern group analysis shows that extension of circle of problems leads to necessity of modification and enhancement of applied tools.

Another natural direction is generalization of the “contraction concept” to conservation laws of (systems of) diffusion equations that is considered in the next part [13] of this series.
